title: Anxiety, Fear & Avoidance
description: Explore when the body alarms before the mind through dialogue, evidence and psychological reasoning.

lessons.title: The feeling isn't the forecast
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of when the body alarms before the mind.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Anxiety can link bodily arousal with threat interpretations. Attention to each heartbeat may make the sensation more noticeable, which can strengthen the belief that something dangerous is happening. A racing heart is an observation; collapse is a prediction that requires additional evidence.

New, severe or concerning physical symptoms warrant appropriate medical assessment. A psychological explanation must not substitute for evaluating physical risk.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), A Cognitive Approach to Panic; NICE CG113.

nodes.title: Try a different response
nodes.prompt: The goal is to improve the situation without pretending that you can read the person's mind.
nodes.explanation: A proportionate response deals with the actual situation: First check for concerning symptoms; if safe, distinguish what is happening in the body from what you fear will follow. Its value does not depend on the other person accepting an interpretation of their motives.
nodes.counterexample: Some situations require independent support or safer channels rather than another direct conversation. New, severe or concerning physical symptoms warrant appropriate medical assessment. A psychological explanation must not substitute for evaluating physical risk.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), A Cognitive Approach to Panic; NICE CG113.

lessons.title: What would change your mind?
lessons.teach: An initial explanation is useful only if it can be challenged. Revisit the characters, test a rival account and apply the idea in another setting. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Test an account of when the body alarms before the mind with new evidence and transfer it to a new case.

nodes.prompt: Which conclusion accounts for both perspectives without confusing an interpretation with a fact?
nodes.explanation: Each character can be responding to a different meaning of the same event. The immediate issue is still observable. Understanding both viewpoints helps explain the conflict without requiring both interpretations to be equally accurate.
